prize_parts.citation: for a body of work that renews lyric, verse narrative and essay through hybrid forms, and that sustains a dialogue with antiquity, grief and the fragment.

statement.case_for: Carson has one of the most unmistakable voices on the list. Autobiography of Red recasts the Geryon myth as a verse novel. Nox builds an elegy from fragments, philological commentary and the physical book. Both books are formal inventions that carry real emotional and intellectual weight, so the formal side is not decoration. The work shows decades of engagement with Greek and Latin texts, and she keeps returning to grief, desire and the limits of translation. This gives the oeuvre a coherent method that develops from book to book. The case rests on distinctiveness of voice, formal achievement and imaginative depth across poetry, essay, drama and translation-linked writing. It does not rest on one celebrated title. Because the work is in English and often brief, a good deal of it can be assessed with fewer translation losses than for several other candidates. This is a judgment from public knowledge, not a fresh reading of the full corpus.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that much of Carson's achievement lies in hybrid, allusive and book-object forms. These are hard to weigh against more conventional sustained oeuvres, and parts of them may depend on classical scholarship or on visual and performance elements that a text-only assessment cannot capture. Her translations and adaptations also blur which works count as her own oeuvre for a citation. Whether quality holds across the later, more occasional output as it does in the best-known books remains an open question. Cărtărescu offers the larger and more consolidated corpus, and that is a serious competing claim.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Carson second and says the real question is whether the whole body of work sustains literary depth beyond Autobiography of Red and Nox. He also notes that her translations and adaptations of classical texts complicate what counts as her own oeuvre.
responses.response: I take both points seriously and cannot dismiss them from public knowledge alone. My answer is that the translations and adaptations are not a separate category. They belong to the same project of treating the classical text as a fragment to be reworked, and a citation can name that scope without crediting translation as such. On depth beyond the two famous books, I agree the burden is real. It is a reason to ask colleagues who know the wider output to test the claim, not a reason to treat the best-known books as a stand-in. I do not want to settle the matter by pointing at those two titles.

responses.point: Mattson puts Cărtărescu first, as a long, coherent visionary project with a late-career peak in the large novels. She also puts Michon second for compressed, wrought prose of exceptional linguistic quality, while acknowledging that the compression suits a modest body of work.
responses.response: Mattson is right that Cărtărescu's scale and coherence are a strong fit for an assessment of the whole oeuvre, and that is why he is my first alternative. Where I differ is that I want his length and encyclopedic density tested against sustained quality. She raises the same worry herself, and I cannot resolve it from translations. On Michon, I agree the voice and syntax are exceptional, but I ranked him lower. The size of the corpus limits the evidence for range and development, and the Swedish and other translations probably lose a great deal of what makes him remarkable. That weakens the claim that his work is assessable across a whole oeuvre, more than it weakens the quality of the prose.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first and Carson second. She doubts whether Carson's reliance on classical and scholarly allusion travels across readers, and whether her hybrid, visual and translation work can sit within a purely textual Nobel standard.
responses.response: I accept that Carson's allusiveness narrows how directly she reaches some readers, and the visual book-object elements are a real difficulty. I would still distinguish difficulty of reference from limited significance. Her central books work through their emotional and formal movement without requiring the reader to hold the source texts in mind, though a deeper reading is richer for knowing them. I agree that the citation should concentrate on the written, lyric and narrative achievement and not on the book-object elements. That is why the proposed citation names lyric, verse narrative and essay.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Carson first. He sees the formal inventiveness as sustained and the dialogue with antiquity as real intellectual depth, and he cautions that critical consensus on the later work is still forming.
responses.response: I agree with the substance of his case and share the caution. A claim to lasting significance that rests on formal invention depends on the later work, where consensus is still forming. The committee should say openly that its confidence in the later output is lower than in the central books. I would not read agreement between us as evidence of merit. The case has to rest on the texts and on the critical record, not on how many members rank her first.

uncertainties: How far Carson's genre-crossing and book-object works can be judged as literature on the page alone, and how much weight performance and limited-edition formats should carry.
How to separate her translations and classical scholarship from the creative oeuvre when drafting a single-writer citation.
Whether the quality of her later, more occasional work matches the central books. My knowledge of the full corpus is partial and rests on public knowledge, not independent verification.
Whether Cărtărescu's very long novels sustain their quality, and how much of the Romanian prose density survives translation. This bears on whether he is the stronger oeuvre-wide candidate.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My own fiction draws on myth and ekphrasis, and I wrote the Lagerlöf biography. I treat both as context only. They are not evidence that I favour any candidate, and no personal tie to any shortlisted writer is documented in the profile.
